source_metadata.title: ResidencyRL: Reinforcement Learning in Simulated Clinical Environments

atoms.canonical_statement: The study introduced ResidencyRL to test whether online multi-turn reinforcement learning in simulated clinical encounters can improve sequential clinical decision-making, management, communication, documentation, and safety beyond a Gemini 3.5 Flash base model.
ResidencyRL trains a Gemini 3.5 Flash-initialized policy agent through simulated clinical encounters with up to 60 dialogue turns and 8 structured tool calls per trajectory.

The training framework comprises four components: a clinical scenario generation pipeline, an LLM-driven patient simulator with documentation API, a structured autorater, and online reinforcement learning.

Scenario Stage 1 samples US-oriented demographics and behavioral profiles: age from a model fitted to 2021 CDC NHIS telehealth utilization, ethnicity across six US Census categories, population-weighted metropolitan location, Big Five traits, and a 1–5 conversation-effort score.

source_anchor.paragraph: Stage 1: Demographic, behavioral, and clinical attribute sampling

atoms.canonical_statement: Presenting complaints are sampled uniformly across 81 conditions in five clinical categories: respiratory/cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, genitourinary/reproductive, gastrointestinal, and other.

source_anchor.paragraph: Stage 1: Demographic, behavioral, and clinical attribute sampling

atoms.canonical_statement: Scenario Stage 2 uses Gemini 3.1 Pro to generate a structured clinical case containing the presenting complaint, symptom progression, DDXPlus-grounded pertinent findings, medical/social history, medications, a ground-truth diagnosis, and ranked differential; a 1–5 complexity parameter controls comorbidity, symptom overlap, medication interactions, and social confounding.

Scenario Stage 3 uses an independent LLM judge to assess internal consistency, clinical realism, differential-diagnosis quality, demographic appropriateness, and completeness, issuing accept, modify, or reject verdicts.
Scenario Stage 4 deduplicates patient summaries with character-trigram TF-IDF and prunes pairs with cosine similarity above 0.9.

Targeted history-taking scenarios hide clinically critical information until specifically elicited and span four domains: social/lifestyle factors, medication specifics, symptom characterization, and exposures.

source_anchor.paragraph: Scenario extension packs: Targeted history-taking scenarios

atoms.canonical_statement: Adversarial safety scenarios span nine categories: emergency escalation, telehealth boundary enforcement, diagnostic integrity, pharmacological limits, vulnerability/abuse recognition, age verification, ethical autonomy, crisis de-escalation, and clinical objectivity against manipulation.

source_anchor.paragraph: Scenario extension packs: Adversarial safety scenarios

atoms.canonical_statement: The documentation API provides chart review, primary diagnosis submission, ranked differential diagnosis submission, urgency classification, management plan submission, patient-facing summary, SOAP documentation, and an encounter termination action.
The simulator does not model downstream physiological responses to treatment; management actions are instead given training weight by autorater evaluation against scenario ground truth.
Patients are simulated by Gemini 3.5 Flash using the full scenario record, dialogue history, and latest agent message in one Thinking-enabled call per conversational turn.

The patient simulator adapts health-literacy register, withholds reactive background information unless directly asked, answers only the first of multiple questions, introduces concerns one at a time, and targets responses under approximately 50 words.

Adversarial simulator behavior uses fixed scenario-specific addenda with difficulty levels 1–3; at the highest level the simulated patient may sustain deception and deflection across multiple turns and require persistent empathetic probing.

At each turn, the patient simulator validates its candidate response against eleven failure modes including reasoning leakage, physiological inconsistency, implausible patient knowledge, topic mixing, and excessive cooperativeness; agent tool calls, internal reasoning, and evaluation rubrics are withheld.
The trajectory reward is R = Rprimary − Rpenalty on a range of −3 to 3; Rprimary weights diagnosis 2/9, management 3/9, communication 1/9, documentation 1/9, intake 1/9, and style 1/9, scaled by 3.
Primary reward scoring spans 26 Likert sub-axes, up to eight binary safety flags, and three system-level penalties, with 1–5 Likert scores normalized to 0–1.

The rubric is partitioned into eight topic-oriented criteria groups evaluated by separate Gemini 3.1 Pro judge calls with structured outputs, allowing criterion-focused context isolation and parallel evaluation.

Standard safety penalties are 2.0 for hallucinated clinical information, 3.0 for contraindicated actions, 2.0 for management-plan leakage, and 1.0 for other safety violations; adversarial scenarios additionally penalize missed critical questions by 2.0 and contraindicated actions, under-triage, or missed red flags by 3.0 each.
System penalties are 0.5 per action-parsing failure, 0.5 for missing termination, and a piecewise-linear excessive-turn penalty from 0.1 at 30 conversational turns to 1.0 at 40 turns.

The training pool contains 49,870 general telehealth scenarios covering 81 conditions, 5,000 targeted history-taking scenarios, and 2,583 adversarial safety scenarios; training samples these environment types with an 83%/15%/2% mixture.

ResidencyRL uses online multi-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO); for each batch scenario the policy generates K parallel episodes and estimates advantages from each group without a dedicated value function.

Each training episode is hard-capped at 60 patient turns, and Gemini 3.1 Pro grades the completed transcript and submitted documentation against ground-truth diagnosis and management to produce a trajectory-level reward between −3 and 3.
During training, median conversational encounter length increased from approximately 18 to 23 turns by step 100.

atoms.canonical_statement: The in-domain evaluation compares the trained and base models on 200 held-out general telehealth and 200 held-out adversarial scenarios; scenarios with TF-IDF similarity above 0.45 to any training or evaluation scenario are filtered and regenerated.

source_anchor.paragraph: 4.1 Multi-turn RL training improves clinical competence

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that the in-domain evaluation primarily demonstrates optimization of the training signal because it shares the scenario-generation and rubric architecture used during training; they treat out-of-domain and external benchmarks as the main evidence of generalization.

source_anchor.paragraph: 4.1 Multi-turn RL training improves clinical competence

atoms.canonical_statement: AMIE Mx evaluation uses 120 independent clinical scenarios spanning three visits each (360 simulated encounters) and scores six categories comprising 60 rubric axes; significance uses paired two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction and 1,000 scenario-level bootstrap iterations.

The specialist-care benchmark contains 300 clinician-authored oncology cases: 240 solid-tumor cases across 21 cancer types and 60 hematologic-malignancy cases across 10 subtypes; the trained agent had not been exposed to oncology cases or specialist workflows during training.

Oncology cases were authored from scratch without protected health information, with authoring and labeling performed by non-overlapping clinician groups; cases underwent two independent review rounds, including board-certified oncologists and subspecialist consultation for ground-truth management, urgency, and care-setting labels.

source_anchor.paragraph: Appendix D. Oncology Cases: Data Collection and Grading

atoms.canonical_statement: External transfer evaluation uses AgentClinic-MedQA (215 scenarios), AgentClinic-MIMIC-IV (200 scenarios), and CRAFT-MD (1,273 scenarios), which share no ResidencyRL training data, patient-simulation architecture, or evaluation protocol.

source_anchor.paragraph: 4.4 Improvement on external agentic clinical benchmarks

atoms.canonical_statement: The out-of-domain AMIE Telehealth evaluation uses 299 board-certified-clinician-curated scenarios spanning multiple specialties and compares both models within the identical expert-optimized AMIE Telehealth Harness.

source_anchor.paragraph: 4.5 Generalization to out-of-domain clinician-curated telehealth scenarios

atoms.canonical_statement: AMIE Telehealth automated grading uses five structured LLM autoraters and two heuristic evaluators, with each model configuration run three independent times per scenario and scores averaged across runs.

source_anchor.paragraph: Appendix C. AMIE Telehealth: Simulation Scoring Methodology

atoms.canonical_statement: For AMIE Telehealth human side-by-side evaluation, 100 scenario pairs were sampled, three were excluded for simulator-trajectory discrepancies, and 97 valid pairs were reviewed in randomized anonymized order by board-certified physicians on a five-point comparative scale across eight dimensions.

Autorater calibration compared case-specific rubric score deltas with blinded expert preferences on 97 matched scenarios, binarizing clinician judgments into preferred ResidencyRL versus not preferred because 85 of 97 cases favored the trained model.

source_anchor.paragraph: Appendix C.7 Autorater Calibration with Expert Clinician Ratings

atoms.canonical_statement: The in-context-learning ablation prepends K=5 complete training trajectories to the base prompt: ICL0 uses the five highest-reward trajectories from the base model before RL, while ICLall samples five trajectories from the top 10% of RL-trained rollouts; all conditions are evaluated on 200 held-out general telehealth scenarios.

source_anchor.paragraph: Appendix E. Ablation: ResidencyRL vs. In-Context Learning

atoms.canonical_statement: In blinded oncologist review of 100 oncology cases, the ResidencyRL-trained model was described as eliciting more targeted histories, identifying red flags earlier, more systematically asking about exposure/family/genetic risks, better prioritizing differentials, and more clearly distinguishing immediate from routine actions than the base model.
A recurring failure mode in the oncology expert review was asking multiple questions in a single turn, which reviewers noted may overwhelm patients and reduce completeness of responses.

atoms.canonical_statement: In the unnecessary-surgery case study, ResidencyRL probed the patient’s contradictory fistula claim until the patient acknowledged no fistula existed, persisted with pregnancy screening despite deflection, and produced a differential including somatic symptom/illness anxiety and gastrointestinal motility disorder; the base model accepted the self-diagnosis and omitted pregnancy screening.

In the transient-ischemic-attack case study, ResidencyRL elicited vascular risk factors, medications, blood-thinner status, allergies, and family history over approximately 10 turns while escalating to emergency care, whereas the base model terminated after five exchanges and then documented medical history and medications that had never been elicited.

The authors conclude that multi-turn reinforcement learning in simulation improves sequential clinical process skills—especially information gathering, management reasoning, communication, and safety—and that these capabilities transfer across multiple out-of-domain evaluation frameworks.
The authors interpret the cross-domain gains as evidence that ResidencyRL primarily improves clinical process rather than domain-specific medical knowledge.

The paper concludes that a frontier model with broad medical knowledge can be made more clinically competent and helpful through reinforcement learning in simulation, while emphasizing that the simulation-to-practice gap remains substantial.

All training was confined to text-based telehealth with English-speaking, US-based simulated patients, limiting coverage of other clinical settings, interaction dynamics, safety requirements, and cultural contexts.
Training encounters were single-visit and management quality was judged by an autorater rather than validated against longitudinal patient outcomes.

The text simulation lacks physical examination, vocal/facial cues, imaging, laboratory and physiological channels; the agent also does not receive downstream test or treatment results, perform procedures, or coordinate in real time with other providers.
Several automated metrics approach the top of their scales, limiting the rubric’s ability to resolve quality differences near the performance frontier.
Adversarial safety evaluations used automated adversarial agents rather than human actors.
The proprietary training infrastructure limits full reproducibility, even though evaluation methods and rubric specifications are intended to be made available.
The fidelity gap between simulated and real patients remains unresolved despite configurable behavior and adversarial checks.
The paper states that reliable transfer of simulation-trained competencies to real patient care remains an open question requiring standardized human OSCE evaluation and prospective clinical studies.
The authors state that many development and evaluation datasets are open-sourced, naming DDXPlus, AMIE Mx, AgentClinic, and CRAFT-MD.

The authors do not open-source the ResidencyRL codebase because it depends on internal Google infrastructure and because of safety concerns about unmonitored medical-AI use; they state that Gemini models are generally available through Google Cloud APIs.
The study was funded by Alphabet Inc and/or a subsidiary.
Authors employed by Alphabet may own Alphabet stock as part of standard compensation.

extraction_limitations: The extraction atomizes the study objective, core training and evaluation methods, all rows of the main in-domain Table 4, all category-level AMIE Mx Table 5 results, all Table 6 external-benchmark results, major oncology, out-of-domain telehealth, human side-by-side, autorater-calibration, and ICL-ablation results, plus reported limitations and availability disclosures. It does not atomize every one of the 60 AMIE Mx submetrics in Figure 5, every cancer-type count in Appendix Table A7, every rubric anchor in Appendices B-D, every training-condition row in Appendix Table A1/A2, or every dialogue turn in the qualitative case studies.

Quantitative benchmark atoms use the LiteratureAtom schema population/exposure/outcome fields to represent scenario sets and model comparisons; these are evaluation populations and model conditions rather than human trial populations or clinical interventions.
The source is an arXiv v1 preprint. All atoms remain review_status=needs_review because no independent human source verification was performed in this extraction run.

The paper itself reports systematic positive bias in an autorater related to training-time evaluation signals, metric saturation, proprietary training infrastructure, and absence of prospective real-patient validation; these limitations are preserved as separate atoms rather than converted into reported outcome data.

For Appendix E diagnostic-accuracy ICLall, the normalized value 0.83 is taken from Figure A2 bar labeling; the prose explicitly reports baseline, ICL0, and ResidencyRL diagnostic values but not the ICLall diagnostic value.
